title: The morning blessings
hookLine: a chain of thanks for waking: sight, clothing, standing upright

lines: BEFORE COFFEE, A LOT WENT RIGHT.
cards: Before coffee, before the phone, before anyone has said a word to you, a lot has already gone right. Your eyes opened. You could tell it was morning.
You sat up, found something to wear, and your feet held you when you stood. None of it feels like news. It's the floor the day is built on, and nobody thanks a floor.
The Jewish morning service thanks it anyway, one piece at a time: a short chain of blessings, each fitted to something a waking body just did.

teach.b: In Hebrew they're called birchot hashachar, the blessings of the dawn. Each opens with baruch atah, blessed are you, then names one gift. Who opens the eyes of the blind.
Who clothes the naked. Who raises up the bowed down. Who makes firm a person's steps.
The Talmud, in tractate Berakhot, page sixty b, walks through a person's waking. When you hear the rooster, say this.
When you open your eyes, when you sit up, when you dress, when you stand, when your feet touch the ground, when you put on your shoes: a blessing for each motion, said at the moment it happened.

teach.h: FROM THE BEDROOM TO THE SERVICE.
teach.b: So in the Talmud's telling, these blessings belong to the bedroom, not the synagogue. Over the centuries many communities moved them into the service and said them as a list.
One explanation: hands weren't yet washed at the bedside, and not everyone knew the words, so the leader said them aloud and everyone answered amen.
Maimonides didn't like the change; he held that each blessing belongs to its own moment. Today some people say a few at home as they wake, and many say them together in the service.
Either way, the order still follows a body getting up.
Underneath is a simple rule: the Talmud teaches that a person shouldn't enjoy anything in this world without a blessing, and waking up is the first thing you enjoy.
Sight and steady legs aren't small just because they're common.

how: Many Jews say the morning blessings at the start of the weekday and Shabbat morning service, often led aloud by the prayer leader with the congregation answering amen, and some say them at home on waking.

games.q: you lead prayers long ago. many people in the room don't know the morning blessings by heart. what do you do?
o: skip them in public; they belong at home.
say them aloud and let everyone answer amen.
wait until everyone has memorized them.
games.why: many communities did just this: the leader said the blessings aloud and the congregation answered amen. it's one reason a bedside practice ended up in the prayer book.

practice: Start with the breath, going in and out without being asked, then pick two more things your body does: your eyes taking in the room, your hands, your heartbeat. Stay a few breaths with each and notice it working.
If you pray, begin each with baruch atah, blessed are you; if not, a plain thank you is enough.

wordCard.voice: Birchot hashachar. The blessings of the dawn: a chain of short thanks for waking, seeing, dressing and standing.

orig.note: Hebrew: blessings of the dawn. shachar is the first light of morning.

carryVoice: Your line: thanks for the basics. Nobody thanks a floor, but this chain of blessings does. Until tomorrow.
